overview: This file documents a 1949 effort by the U.S. occupation authorities in Japan to restore commercial wire telephone service between Japan and Korea over the submarine cable linking Fukuoka and Busan (then spelled Pusan). It contains the covering despatch from the United States Political Adviser for Japan, a diplomatic note forwarding the Japanese Government’s proposal, an interoffice check sheet recording Civil Communications Section and G-2 consideration, and a technical memorandum on the cable network’s wartime and postwar condition. The proposed “sender keep all” arrangement would allow each country to retain charges collected domestically, avoiding the absence of a workable exchange rate between the Japanese yen and Korean won; the documents also reveal plans for U.S. occupation censorship personnel to monitor approximately one quarter of non-privileged calls.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 429 on reopening Japan–Korea telephone service
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State; copy to the American Embassy, Seoul
subfiles.about: The covering despatch transmits occupation-authority correspondence concerning the proposed restoration of commercial wire telephone service between Japan and Korea.
subfiles.summary: The chargé d’affaires ad interim forwards a diplomatic note presenting the Japanese Government’s proposal to reopen the Fukuoka–Pusan submarine-cable telephone circuit on a “sender keep all” basis. It also transmits a Civil Communications Section request and supporting records, including G-2’s statement that it had no objection. Korean diplomatic representatives in Japan had informally expressed eagerness for restoration, making reopening likely once technical problems were resolved.

subfiles.title: Diplomatic note forwarding the Japanese telephone proposal
subfiles.from: Diplomatic Section, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: The Diplomatic Section formally forwards a Japanese proposal to reopen commercial telephone service between Fukuoka and Busan.
subfiles.summary: The note explains that the Japan–Korea telephone service was suspended at the end of the war, although Japanese sources believed the submarine cable remained in good condition. Japan proposed that each side retain the revenue from calls originating in its territory, as was already done for wire telegraph traffic. The arrangement was recommended both to make the service broadly available and to avoid foreign-exchange settlement problems, and the Korean Mission was asked to obtain and transmit its government’s reply.

subfiles.title: CCS check sheet and G-2 concurrence on restoring the cable circuit
subfiles.from: Civil Communications Section (CCS), with endorsement by G-2 dated June 9, 1949
subfiles.to: Civil Section (CS), via G-2; endorsement returned to CCS via the Diplomatic Section
subfiles.about: An interoffice check sheet recommends referring the proposed Japan–Korea telephone arrangement to Korean authorities and records G-2’s approval.
subfiles.summary: The Civil Communications Section reports demand for restoring the prewar Fukuoka–Pusan telephone service and states that Japanese sources considered the cables serviceable. Information attributed to the U.S. Army Forces in Korea indicated that Korean communications authorities were also interested. CCS recommends the “sender keep all” basis because no usable international exchange rate existed between the yen and won; on June 9, G-2 recorded that it had no objection to reopening the circuit.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on cable conditions, traffic, censorship, and regional circuits
subfiles.to: For the record; circulated between G-2 and the Civil Communications Section
subfiles.about: The memorandum reviews the condition and use of Japan–Korea telephone cables, proposed censorship coverage, and other surviving or defunct international cable routes.
subfiles.summary: At Japan’s surrender, two telephone circuits ran from Fukuoka through Tsushima to Busan, one continuing by landline to Seoul; the latter carried about thirty public calls per month initially, falling to roughly five before public use ended in mid-1946. The Japanese authorities continued maintaining and testing the lines, while occupation censorship personnel retained monitoring capability. The memorandum states that approximately 25 percent of non-privileged calls on a restored circuit would be monitored and that South Korea would decide whether Busan or Seoul served as the terminus. It also inventories other links—to San Francisco, Vladivostok, Shimonoseki, and Wonsan via Ulleungdo—and recommends G-2 concurrence as consistent with SCAP policy on reopening Japan’s external communications.

interest: The file offers an unusually detailed view of how a seemingly routine postwar telephone link involved diplomacy, engineering, currency policy, military intelligence, and occupation censorship. Particularly valuable are the surviving traffic figures, the proposed 25-percent monitoring rate, and the explanation that Japan had continued maintaining the circuits despite never receiving formal notice of their suspension. The memorandum also provides a compact inventory of East Asian cable routes—including links toward the Soviet Union and North Korea—and shows how the restoration of civilian communications remained embedded in SCAP security policy.
